Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Helio Head of Platform), Erik Johnson (ML Eng), Maya Patel (Security), Alex Rivera (Product), Sam Cole (Infra)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood did a focussed Optimize walkthrough centered on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for Helio Payments' conversational routing and fraud-detection use cases. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and cost, dedicated vs hosted options for predictable throughput, and security/compliance asks (SOC2, KMS/HSM, VPC peering). Agreed next steps: share pricing worksheet, run a 48h benchmark on a dedicated slot, and send security pack.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia Martinez from Redwood, with Liam Chen our solutions engineer. Today we wanted to walk through Redwood Optimize specifically batching and KV/prefix cache recs and then a simple cost model for the numbers you shared.

[00:00:18] Priya (Helio): Thanks Sofia. We're most interested in the fraud detection flow and the chat routing where latency spikes are most visible. We shared a sample of traces earlier this week.

[00:00:32] Liam (Redwood SE): Yep saw the traces, thanks. Quick agenda: 1) short primer on continuous batching and how it maps to your throughput; 2) prefix / KV cache patterns and when to use each; 3) cost model walk-through; 4) Q&A and next steps.

[00:00:50] Erik (ML): One ask up front — we need to keep tail latency under 200ms 95th for the chat routing. Fraud detection can tolerate a bit more, like 500ms 95th.

[00:01:05] Sofia: Good to know. We'll show how batching/gating and cached prefixes can keep cost lower without breaking your SLOs. Also we'll call out Dedicated options if you need predictable tail behavior.

[00:01:30] Liam: Quick primer — continuous batching is basically holding a tiny window to group tokens across inflight requests. On GPUs we trigger kernels more efficiently when batch sizes hit sweet spots. For Helio's traffic, we saw a lot of many short conversations and a heavy tail of long sessions — so the trick is adaptive batch windows plus prefix caching for common system prompts.

[00:02:05] Alex (Product): When you say prefix cache do you mean the K V cache thing or a textual prefix cache?

[00:02:12] Liam: Good question, both concepts exist. Textual prefix cache is reusing the same prompt tokens server-side; KV cache is keeping the model's key/value activations in memory between calls for the same session or similar context. For your gateway flows, prefix caching reduces repeated token decode cost; KV cache reduces repeated self-attention compute for continuing conversations.

[00:02:45] Priya: There's also our PII masking step which reconstructs prompts — will that break caching?

[00:02:53] Liam: It depends — if you normalize and canonicalize prompts before the cache key, you can still hit the cache. We often recommend a light pre-normalization layer in the gateway to increase cache hit rates without leaking sensitive tokens.

[00:03:20] Maya (Security): On that note, anything cached in-memory — we need to know retention and encryption. If it's persistent KV cache on Dedicated we need guidance on HSM integration.

[00:03:33] Sofia: We'll provide the KMS/HSM integration doc. Short answer: persistent KV entries can be encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys in Private or Dedicated. For hosted, we offer envelope encryption and rotation logs; for Private you control keys.

[00:04:00] Sam (Infra): Your autoscaling jitter — how do you prevent batching windows from ballooning under load? We can't have latency suddenly jump.

[00:04:12] Liam: There are two levers: max_batch_delay (ms) and min_batch_size. Our default adaptive strategy keeps max_batch_delay low for latency-sensitive routes. If you need sub-200ms 95th we'd set max_batch_delay to ~10-20ms and use smaller min_batch_size. For high throughput fraud jobs you can relax those to get better amortization.

[00:04:40] Erik: Can you show some numbers? The sample spreadsheet you referenced earlier — how did you derive cost savings?

[00:04:48] Liam: Yup, let's open the cost model. (note: link shared in chat: https://redwood.app/optimize/worksheets/helio-1) High level: cost per 1M tokens is a function of token/sec throughput, GPU utilization (batching increases util), and KV cache hit rate (reduces compute per request). For Helio we modeled two routes — chat routing (low tokens per request, high QPS) and fraud detection (higher tokens, lower QPS).

[00:05:20] [00:05:30] Liam: Example numbers from the model — with no caching and conservative batching we see $X baseline (redacted in transcript), with prefix cache hit ~30% and KV cache hit ~20% we drop per-token cost by ~18-25%. With more aggressive caching and a dedicated pool you can get to ~35% unit cost reduction. These are estimates — we'll run a benchmark to validate.

[00:06:05] Priya: That 35% sounds great. What's the tradeoff for the chat route at peak hours?

[00:06:12] Liam: You trade off some cold-start latency on first-turn for a much lower steady-state cost. For chat routing specifically, prefix cache for prompts like system messages and canned templates gives you consistent wins. For sessions where KV cache is sticky (user has many interactions) you see better tail behavior on Dedicated because KV is kept warm across GPUs in that mode.

[00:06:45] Maya: What about model variants when fallback happens — do you route automatically to smaller quantized models?

[00:06:52] Sofia: Yes, smart routing policies can fall back to cost-optimized quantized variants if capacity is constrained. You can set soft SLO thresholds per route; Redwood will attempt the primary model and if latency or cost thresholds are at risk, it will route to a compatible variant.

[00:07:18] Alex: For our compliance folks it's important to see audit trails of who changed routing policies.

[00:07:24] Sofia: Console has RBAC and an audit log that records changes, rollouts, and who triggered them. We'll include screenshots in the packet.

[00:07:40] Erik: Back to numbers — in the spreadsheet I see assumptions about average token lengths and session lengths. Those came from our traces, right?

[00:07:48] Liam: Correct, we derived per-route token distributions from the traces you uploaded and then ran a synthetic binning to estimate batching efficiency. If you provide a longer window of traces we can improve the model fidelity.

[00:08:16] [00:08:30] Liam: Let me talk through a concrete example: chat routing — we assumed 150 QPS, average request 32 tokens. With adaptive batching at a 15ms max delay, we hit average batch sizes of ~18 tokens which maps to GPU util of ~45% on a A100-like profile. Add prefix cache at 40% hit rate, and you remove ~35% of repeated forward passes. The net effect is unit cost down ~22% and 95th latency marginally impacted if you tune the delay.

[00:09:05] Priya: And for fraud detection?

[00:09:08] Liam: Fraud detection — lower QPS, avg 220 tokens per request. Batching yields less relative benefit but KV cache helps when you have repeated partial context or reruns. On Dedicated you get predictability so your 95th is more stable.

[00:09:35] Priya: ROI question — what's the threshold where Dedicated is worth it? We have seasonal spikes.

[00:09:42] Sofia: Rough rule: if you have sustained utilization above 60-70% of a single dedicated pool for many hours per day, Dedicated becomes cost-effective because reserved capacity and pinned KV warm state reduce unit costs. We'll calculate a breakeven in the worksheet for your traffic patterns.

[00:10:05] Maya: Security follow-up: for Private deployment in our VPC, does Redwood run any control plane that needs peering, or is it fully customer managed?

[00:10:14] Sofia: For Private we run a control plane that can be operated as managed or customer-hosted. Networking models include VPC peering, direct connect, or air-gapped on-prem packages. We'll send the network diagrams and the SOC2 material.

[00:10:35] Sam: On the bench — how do you simulate user patterns? We want the benchmark to be realistic.

[00:10:40] Liam: We replay traces with time-of-day QPS profiles and vary token distributions. For the dedicated benchmark we'll bring up a mirrored load that approximates your 7-day sample. We'll keep metric tagging so you can compare latency percentiles and cost per successful request.

[00:11:05] Erik: Any gotchas we should expect? For example, cold KV misses causing big spikes?

[00:11:12] Liam: Cold misses are the main one — they can cause single request slowdowns. We mitigate via warmers, prefetch policies for known sessions, and smart fallback rules. Also ensure model and quantization choices align with desired accuracy — aggressive quantization can save cost but reduce some hallucination/accuracy margins.

[00:11:40] Priya: Do you have any examples where prefix caching backfired?

[00:11:45] Liam: It can backfire if your prompts are highly personalized with user-specific tokens that shouldn't be cached. That's why we recommend canonicalization and strict cache key hygiene. Also logging — make sure your cache metrics are surfaced so you can detect negative regressions.

[00:12:05] [00:12:30] Sofia: Quick demo in the console here — showing per-route cost breakdown, cache hit dashboards, and a sample rollout policy with a canary that adjusts batch delay. (screen share) You can see a cost slider where we simulate increasing prefix cache hit from 0% to 50% to show unit cost delta.

[00:13:10] Alex: Nice. On the canary, if the canary hits worse errors we can auto-roll back?

[00:13:14] Liam: Yes, automatic rollback rules and alert hooks. We integrate with PagerDuty and Slack.

[00:13:30] Maya: We'll need logged evidence for audits showing key rotation and who accessed KMS.

[00:13:36] Sofia: Included in the security pack.

[00:13:50] [00:14:00] (brief cross talk, screen unshared)

[00:14:18] Priya: Okay, practical next step is the 48h benchmark on a dedicated slot. We want to see 95th latencies for chat and fraud routes, plus per-route cost delta.

[00:14:30] Liam: We'll stand that up. For the benchmark we need an anonymized trace and any canonicalization rules you want to apply. Also confirm whether we should test hosted or private network config.

[00:14:45] Priya: Start with hosted dedicated pool and then test Private if the first run looks good. We'll get the trace to you by EOD tomorrow.

[00:15:00] Sofia: Great. A couple of final Qs — any procurement blockers we should be aware of?

[00:15:08] Alex: Legal will need data residency and DPA clauses, but that's standard. Maya might flag HSM requirement.

[00:15:20] Maya: HSM for the encryption keys would be preferred for production. Also we'll need a periodic attestations cadence.

[00:15:28] Sofia: Understood — we'll include HSM options in the security doc and outline attestation cadence.

[00:15:45] Erik: One last thing — when you run the cost model, can you provide sensitivity to cache hit rates? We'd like a table that shows unit cost at 0%, 20%, 40%, 60% cache hits.

[00:15:56] Liam: Absolutely — we'll produce that and include it in the worksheet.

[00:16:10] Priya: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.

[00:16:15] Sofia: Thanks all, recap: Liam runs 48h benchmark, Priya to provide traces, Sofia sends pricing worksheet and security pack, Maya to confirm KMS/HSM requirements. Follow-up meeting next Tue.

[00:16:30] (call ends)
